title: K-B-D

cards: Some people leave a meeting and nobody notices the empty chair. Others step out for a minute and the whole room goes off balance, as if something heavy has been lifted off the table.
English says it too: his word carries weight. We talk about importance as if it had mass. Hebrew builds the idea into a root.
The same three letters that mean heavy also mean honor. Kaf, vet, dalet: K-B-D.

teach.b: Turn it four ways. First, heavy. Israel is fighting Amalek, and Moses stands on a hill with his hands raised.
While they're up, Israel prevails; when they drop, Amalek does. "But Moses' hands were heavy." Heavy is kaved, from this root.
So Aaron and Hur put a stone under him to sit on and hold up his hands, one on each side, until the sun goes down. Second, honor.

teach.h: HONOR: THY FATHER AND THY MOTHER.
teach.b: "Honour thy father and thy mother." Honor is kabed, the very same letters. To honor a parent, in the root's own picture, is to treat them as heavy: not easy to brush aside.
When Moses goes up Sinai, "the glory of the LORD abode upon mount Sinai," and a cloud covers the mountain. Glory is kavod: presence that settles and doesn't drift off. Fourth, the twist.

teach.h: WHO IS HONORED? WHO HONORS OTHERS.
teach.b: In Pirkei Avot, Ben Zoma, whom you met on day two hundred sixty-five asking who is wise, asks: who is honored? The one who honors other people. You don't get weight by demanding it.
You get it by giving it. A tired man's arms, a parent, a cloud, a sage's question. Honor, in Hebrew, isn't a title.
It's how much someone weighs to you: whether their words land, or blow away.

how: Kibbud av va'em, honoring father and mother, is a commandment Jews study and practice in detail; and the word kavod, honor, is used in daily Jewish life for the respect owed to every person.

o: a root meaning high, as in rank and a throne
a root meaning bright, as in light and fame
a root meaning heavy, and so honor and glory

p: heavy, held up by Aaron and Hur
who is honored? who honors others

s: in Hebrew, heavy and honor come from the same three letters
kaved and kavod both come from K-B-D.
in the battle with Amalek, Moses' hands grew light and floated up
they were heavy; Aaron and Hur held them up until sunset.
Ben Zoma says the honored one is whoever others honor
he says it's the one who honors other people.

games.q: you're Aaron, on the hill. Moses' raised hands are getting heavy, and the battle turns when they drop. what do you do?
o: tell Moses to rest and hope for the best.
put a stone under him and hold up his hands.
run down to join the fight.
games.why: Aaron and Hur sit him on a stone and hold his hands steady, one on each side, until the sun goes down.

practice: Let your hands rest heavy in your lap and feel their weight. Bring to mind someone whose words you tend to skim, a parent, a coworker, an older neighbor who tells the same story twice, and recall one thing they said lately.
This time let it land and weigh what it weighs, and if you pray, hold them in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: K-B-D. Kaf, vet, dalet: the root of kaved, heavy, and kavod, honor and glory. To honor is to give weight. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: honor, glory; from the root K-B-D, heavy.

carryVoice: Your line: honor is weight. Heavy hands, and two friends who held them up. Until tomorrow.
